title: Two Umbrellas
author: Tadoku Note (original)
summary: 雨の日、駅で傘を取り違えた二人。傘を返そうとするたびに、すれ違いが続きます。小さな恋の物語。

source.note: Original text written for this app.

paragraphs: It was raining hard on the Tuesday that Hana took the wrong umbrella.

She was in a hurry. She worked in a small design office near Kichijoji Station, and she was late for an important meeting. At the station, there was an umbrella stand by the door of the coffee shop where she always bought her morning coffee. She put her umbrella in the stand, bought her coffee, picked up her umbrella and ran out into the rain.

It was only at lunchtime that she looked at it carefully. Her umbrella was dark blue. This one was dark blue too, but the handle was made of wood, and there was a small name tag on it. The tag said, in neat handwriting: “If found, please return to the Blue Door Coffee Shop. Thank you. — T.”
Hana felt terrible. That evening, she went back to the coffee shop. It was closed. She went again the next morning, but the shop had a sign on the door: “Closed today. Sorry!”

On Thursday, she finally found it open. A tall young man was behind the counter. He had paint on his fingers and a pencil behind his ear. “Excuse me,” Hana said. “I think I took someone’s umbrella on Tuesday. It has a tag that says ‘T.’”

The young man looked at the umbrella and smiled. “That’s mine,” he said. “I’m Taku. My uncle owns this shop. I help him sometimes. On Tuesday, I found this umbrella in the stand.” He took out a dark blue umbrella with a plastic handle. It was hers.
They exchanged umbrellas and laughed. “They look almost the same,” said Hana.
“Almost,” said Taku. “But yours has a little cat on the button.” He showed her. She had never noticed it.

That could have been the end of the story. But the next week, it rained again. And when Hana left the coffee shop, she found a small piece of paper tied to her umbrella handle. On it was a tiny drawing of a cat holding an umbrella. Under it, someone had written: “Don’t take the wrong one today!”
Hana smiled all morning.

The next day, she left a note on the wooden umbrella. It was not a drawing, because she was a designer, not an artist, and she was shy about her drawings. She wrote: “Thank you for the cat. Is it raining in your picture, too?”
On Friday, there was a new drawing on her umbrella: the cat and a small dog, sharing one umbrella in the rain. “It’s always raining in my pictures,” said the note. “I like rain.”

For the next month, they wrote notes to each other on rainy days. On sunny days, there were no umbrellas, and therefore no notes. Hana noticed that she started to check the weather forecast every evening, and hope for rain.
But she never saw Taku at the counter. His uncle was always there instead. She wanted to ask about him, but she felt too shy.

Then, at the beginning of June, the rainy season began. On the first rainy morning, Hana came to the coffee shop, excited. But the wooden umbrella was not in the stand. There was no note. It was the same the next day, and the next.
On the fourth day, she finally spoke to the uncle. “Excuse me. Your nephew, Taku... is he all right?”

The uncle smiled as if he had been waiting for this question. “He’s fine,” he said. “He’s an art student. He’s busy with his final exhibition. It opens this Saturday, in a small gallery near the park.” He gave her a little card.

On Saturday, it was raining. Hana took her umbrella and went to the gallery. It was a small white room with about twenty pictures on the walls. And in every picture, it was raining. There were people under umbrellas on crowded streets. There were cats under umbrellas. There was a coffee shop with an umbrella stand by the door.

In the corner, there was one picture that was different. It showed a woman in a dark blue coat running out of a coffee shop with an umbrella that was not hers. Under it was the title: “The Wrong Umbrella.” Next to the title was a small red sticker. It said: “Not for sale.”
“I couldn’t sell that one,” said a voice behind her.
Hana turned. Taku was standing there, with paint on his fingers and a pencil behind his ear. He looked nervous.
“I wanted to tell you about the exhibition,” he said. “But I didn’t know your name. And it didn’t rain on the right days.”
Hana laughed. “My name is Hana,” she said. “And it’s raining now.”
When they left the gallery, they walked to the station together. They had two umbrellas, but they only used one.
